title: Beats 360 Deliver Customizability and a Revamped Over-Ear Headphone Design
content:
After months of teases and leaks, Beats is officially announcing its new Beats 360 headphone today. Priced at $349.99, Beats 360 represents a rethinking of the Beats over-ear headphone design, with an emphasis on sound quality, comfort, and customizability.

Subscribe to the MacRumors YouTube channel for more videos.

Beats 360 is not a replacement for the brand's Studio Pro over-ear headphone, as the Studio Pro will remain part of the Beats lineup at a reduced price point of $299.99, down from the previous $349.99. Compared to Studio Pro, Beats 360 features a completely new acoustic architecture that delivers up to 1.75× more active noise cancellation and a 12dB increase in output while maintaining clarity across all frequencies with low distortion.

In addition to active noise cancellation (ANC), which utilizes a system of eight microphones to analyze the acoustic environment inside and outside the headphone, Beats 360 also support Transparency mode to still allow you to hear the world around you, while turning off ANC and Transparency activates Adaptive EQ to continually tune acoustic performance.



Personalized Spatial Audio with dynamic head tracking is also supported, allowing users to take full advantage of Apple's platforms that deliver 360-degree Dolby Atmos sound and move within the sound field as they turn their heads.
"Beats didn't just participate in the rise of over-ear headphones—we helped define the category," said Oliver Schusser, Apple's vice president of Music, Sports, and Beats. "Beats 360 is the next chapter of that story. We combined our most advanced acoustic performance ever with a perfectly balanced design that moves effortlessly with you. And with our new interchangeable cushions, our customers can express themselves in a way no other over-ear headphone can."
Beats 360 is available in four color options: Black, Cloud (an off-white), Pink, and Sky (a light blue). It includes comfortable color-matched Perfomance Knit ear and headband cushions, but the cushions are removable and interchangeable, allowing you to customize your favorite look and even change color combinations to suit the moment. Separate Performance Knit cushion kits are available in all four of the standard colors, plus Volt (a neon yellow-green) and Navy.


The Performance Knit memory foam cushions are breathable and ideal for working out and other active uses, but for the times you might prefer a more traditional cushion style, Beats is also introducing UltraPlush cushion kits in Black and Ivory. Similar to the ones found on Studio Pro and Solo 4, Beats 360 UltraPlush cushions feature a more pillowy feel with memory foam wrapped in engineered leather. Sensors in Beats 360 identify whether you are using Performance Knit or UltraPlush cushions, and they automatically adjust the acoustic tuning and noise cancellation filtering to maintain a consistent listening experience regardless of cushion material.

Beats 360 in dozens of color combinations

Cushion kits for both Performance Knit and UltraPlush will be priced at $49.99, but for a limited time and in select markets (US, UK, Canada, Australia, France, China, and South Korea), Beats is offering a launch promo that drops cushion kit pricing to just $9.99 or the rough equivalent in the local currency. Swapping out cushions is as simple as a quick twist on each ear cushion to remove and install, while the headband cushion snaps off and on with a small amount of effort while remaining securely attached during use.

Beats 360 in Sky

For active users, Beats 360 is the first Beats over-ear headphone product to feature an IPX4 sweat and water resistance rating, meaning it is protected against liquid ingress.

Beats 360 in Sky with Navy cushions

The removable cushions also make it easy to clean them, a welcome feature for those who plan to use Beats 360 for workouts. Beats recommends mixing one teaspoon (5ml) of laundry detergent into one cup (250ml) of water, rubbing the solution onto each cushion with a lint-free cloth for one minute each, wiping them clean with a separate cloth dampened with fresh water, and drying them with another lint-free cloth.



While over-ear and on-ear headphones have generally required thick headbands in order to accommodate multiple cables to connect the two ear cups, Beats 360 actually consists of two independent wireless earphones, with each containing its own battery, antenna and processing circuitry.

As a result, the headband houses only a single power cable to connect the two sides, allowing the batteries in both sides to be charged simultaneously from a single USB-C port. The thin headband also helps to optimize weight distribution, so while Beats 360 and Studio Pro are similar in weight at a little under 300 grams, Beats 360 puts more of the mass into the cushions where it matters most for comfort.

Siri" support is also included.


When it comes to battery life, Beats 360 deliver 32 hours of playback with ANC on, with a five-minute Fast Fuel charge giving you an hour of playback time in a pinch.

iCloud pairing and switching, Audio Sharing to allow a friend with compatible AirPods or Beats to listen to your audio, and Find My support. Android users get many of the same features with one-touch and ecosystem pairing, Audio Switch, and Find Hub geolocation.

Unlike the Beats Studio Pro, Beats 360 headband does not fold for travel, but the earcups do twist flat, and the headphones slide into a woven ripstop carrying case with a magnetic closure and a rear loop to hook onto a finger or carabiner. The case measures about 9 inches square and a little over 2 inches thick at its pleated bottom with the headphone inside. I prefer this flatter style of case to that of the Studio Pro, as it allows the headphone to fit into a computer bag or backpack more easily.

Cases for Beats Studio Pro (left) and Beats 360 (right)

In support of the 360 launch, Beats is debuting a new ad campaign featuring Kendall Jenner, led by a short film of Jenner meeting a friend at a cafe but realizing that everyone in the room is a different version of herself styled with a unique combination of ear cushions, emphasizing the individuality that's possible with Beats 360.


"I'm always on the go and switching between so many different looks," said Kendall Jenner. "So Beats 360 fits my lifestyle. I love that I can switch the cushions to match whatever I'm doing that day."

In a brief interview with Schusser at a Beats preview event earlier this month, he discussed how Jenner was an ideal candidate to promote Beats 360 given the many roles she plays throughout any given day in her personal and professional life.

He also addressed how Beats has been able to flourish under Apple's ownership, with Beats gaining access to all of Apple's expertise in audio as Apple and Beats engineers work side-by-side on products. At the same time, Beats has been able to maintain its own identity on the product design and marketing sides, continuing to focus on active lifestyle and celebrity marketing that remains distinct from how Apple promotes its own products.

available to order starting today at apple.com in the United States and more than 100 other countries and regions, as well as at Amazon and other third-party retailers. Availability follows this Thursday, September 24. It comes with the woven ripstop carrying case, while additional cushion kits, USB-C charging cables, and power adapters are sold separately.

title: Apple’s next-gen photo controls only work on images ‘captured’ on a new iPhone
content:
Macworld





One of the more interesting elements of this month’s Surprise and Shine launch event was Apple’s subtle blurring of the boundary between hardware and software upgrades.
Many of the new health and audio AI features showcased for the Apple Watch Series 12, for instance, felt more like changes Apple would normally discuss in the context of the watchOS update at WWDC. Customers were naturally curious to know what new features they would be able to enjoy on older hardware, and Apple didn’t exactly rush to clarify the situation.
It does now appear, however, that one compatibility pledge has been reversed. Apple initially claimed that new texture and grain controls in the Camera app would be available for anyone with an iPhone 16 or later, provided they update their handset to iOS 27. But as spotted by the Twitter/X user CID, the same page now indicates that these features are exclusive to photos taken with the iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and Duo.


HOLYYY Apple just pulled the biggest SWITCHEROO after 10 DAYS
It seems they will no longer support older iPhones with the new photographic styles i posted this morning pic.twitter.com/08LktWDq2V
— CID (@theonecid) September 22, 2026





“The new texture and grain controls in Photographic Styles will be available on iOS 27 on iPhone 16, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16 Pro…” begins the quoted text in what the poster claims is its original form before an update on September 11. Whereas after the update the same section indicates that the new controls “will be available for photos captured on iPhone 18 Pro models and… iPhone Duo.”
I haven’t been able to find exactly the same wording but I can confirm the change as indicated in a separate document.
At time of writing, Apple’s press release for the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max contains an endnote (4) about compatibility: “The new texture and grain controls will be available for photos captured on iPhone 18 Pro models and the Ultra Wide, Main, and Center Stage cameras on iPhone Duo.”

				
					

				
			
Apple




When I use the Wayback Machine to view an archived version of the same page from September 10, the wording of this note changes drastically: “The new texture and grain controls will be available in iOS 27 on iPhone models that support the latest generation of Photographic Styles. See supported models.” Those last two words are a link to this list which clearly, even now, includes those older handsets.

				
					

				
			As you can see, note 4 has changed significantly.
David Price / Foundry




Indeed Apple appears to have decoupled latest-gen Photographic Styles, a general feature which is still something offered on iPhone 16 and later, from the specific subset of texture and grain controls. These latter features now have a separate compatibility list, and this only contains the iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and Duo. However, that list pertains to the phones’ camera rather than the specific Photographic Styles tools. 
I contacted Apple to seek official confirmation of the change and to ask why this has happened. In a background statement, Apple reiterated the footnote saying photos need to be “captured” on one of the newest iPhones to use the new photographic styles but indicated that older phones will have access to the same editing tools for photos taken with an iPhone 18 Pro or Duo.
So it appears photos need to be taken by one of the newer phones in order to apply the new styles, but the tools themselves will technically be available on the older phones originally listed. Theoretically, you’ll be able to take a photo with a new phone and AirDrop it to an iPhone 17 for editing.
It’s unclear why they would be restricted to the newer phones, since the iPhone Duo essentially has the same camera as the iPhone 17 and 17e. In its press release for the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple says the new A20 Pro processor “features a new Dual 16-core Neural Engine, which accelerates on-device AI models and computational photography,” so it could be related to the new chip, which is only available on those three phones.

title: Apple Planning to Bring iPhone Duo Display Tech to Pro in 2029
content:
Apple's 2029 "Pro" iPhones could adopt thinner and more power-efficient OLED screens, according to UBI Research.


The technology, known as Color Filter on Encapsulation (CoE), removes the conventional polarizer from the ‌OLED‌ panel and places a color filter directly on top of its encapsulation layer. A polarizer helps suppress reflections from ambient light, but it also absorbs a significant portion of the light produced by the display.

Removing the polarizer allows more light to pass through, potentially enabling a display to reach greater brightness without consuming additional power, or use less power while maintaining the same brightness. Eliminating the separate layer can also make the display assembly thinner, freeing up internal space for components such as the battery, cameras, and more.

Samsung's internal testing, its original implementation improved light transmission by 33% and reduced power consumption by up to 25% compared with an ‌OLED‌ panel using a traditional polarizer.

CoE technology presents some technical challenges. Without a polarizer, manufacturers have to control external reflections through a combination of color filters, black pixel-defining layers, low-reflection coatings, and other optical measures. UBI Research believes the difficulty of maintaining outdoor visibility, viewing angles, contrast, and color accuracy may explain why Apple is reportedly waiting until 2029 to bring the technology to its high-volume conventional iPhone models.

iPhone Duo, reports indicated that its Samsung-supplied folding ‌OLED‌ display would use CoE technology. Apple has not detailed the panel's internal construction, but UBI Research sees the foldable device as a potential first step toward using polarizer-free ‌OLED‌ displays across the iPhone "Pro" lineup.

The research firm estimates that annual panel demand for the two Pro models could remain between 90 million and 100 million units, making the proposed transition significantly larger in scale than CoE's use in foldable devices. Samsung Display and LG Display are expected to lead the initial supply, while BOE could compete for orders if it can meet Apple's requirements.

title: Mac Studio 2026: M5 Max and M5 Ultra specs, prices and benchmarks
content:
Macworld






New Mac Studio 2026: At a glance
What’s new: The 2026 Mac Studio gains M5 Max and M5 Ultra chips, dramatically faster AI and graphics performance, faster SSD storage, increased memory bandwidth, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and enhanced professional connectivity. 
Release date: Announced on August 25, 2026
On sale: Shipping from September 22, 2026, but the Mac Studio with 512GB of unified memory is coming in late October.
Price: From $2,499/£2,499
In August 2026, Apple launched a new Mac Studio to replace the M4 Max and M3 Ultra model introduced 17 months previously. The 2026 Mac Studio retains its familiar compact design, but our testing reveals substantial improvements inside – particularly in SSD speed and graphics performance.
The previous generation mixed chip generations, pairing M4 Max with M3 Ultra. The new models bring both tiers into the M5 family: M5 Max offers an 18-core CPU and up to a 40-core GPU, while M5 Ultra scales to a 36-core CPU and 80-core GPU. Both feature Neural Accelerators built into every GPU core to boost AI processing.
Our M5 Max Mac Studio review found approximately 23 percent higher multicore performance in Geekbench 7 and 33 percent higher GPU rendering performance in Cinebench 2024 compared with the tested M4 Max Studio. Storage delivered the biggest leap: our 4TB configuration achieved approximately 2.7 times the read throughput and 2.2 times the write throughput. Results vary by workload, however, with our video export and encoding tests showing more modest improvements.
For M5 Ultra, Apple claims up to 1.3 times the CPU performance, 1.8 times the graphics performance and 4.3 times the AI compute performance of M3 Ultra, depending on the workload and configuration.


When is the new Mac Studio available?
The new Mac Studio with M5 Max and M5 Ultra was announced on August 25, 2026. Shipping of most configurations began on September 22. Apple has confirmed that Mac Studio models configured with 512GB of unified memory will ship in “late October.”
You can order the new Mac Studio from Apple, but you may find it discounted elsewhere.

Higher-priced configurations include an M5 Max with a 40-core GPU and up to 128GB of unified memory, or an M5 Ultra with an 80-core GPU and up to 512GB of unified memory. 
Has the Mac Studio price gone up?
In June 2026, Apple raised the starting price of the Mac Studio by $500, from $1,999 to $2,499. The M3 Ultra model saw an even steeper increase, rising $1,300 from its $3,999 launch price to $5,299. The hikes were part of broader increases across the Mac lineup, which Apple attributed to sharply higher component costs, particularly RAM.
The new M5 Max Mac Studio remains at the June price of $2,499, but the M5 Ultra model has risen by another $200 to $5,499. That makes it $1,500 more expensive than the previous-generation Ultra model was when it launched in March 2025.
Here’s a breakdown of the key price changes for the Mac Studio:


ModelOriginal PriceJune Price M5 Update price
M4 Max, 36GB, 512GB$1,999 / £2,099$2,499 / £2,499$2,499 / £2,499 
M3 Ultra, 96GB, 1TB$3,999 / £4,199 $5,299 / £5,299$5,499 / £5,499 

 



When it comes to high prices, the M5 Ultra Mac Studio is filling the gap left by the removal of the Mac Pro from the line up back in March 2026.


Mac Studio M5 Max and M5 Ultra specs

				
					

				
			
Petter Ahrnstedt




Mac Studio moves to M5 Max and M5 Ultra, with up to a 36-core CPU, 80-core GPU, 512GB unified memory and 1.2TB/s memory bandwidth. Storage now uses PCIe Gen 6 for twice the performance, while connectivity adds Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and USB-C genlock. 
Processor: M5 Ultra and M5 Max chip compared
The Mac Studio comes with either Apple’s Max or Ultra chips. The Max chip is aimed at demanding professional and creative workflows and supports large amounts of unified memory and high memory bandwidth. The Max chip is also available as an option for the MacBook Pro. 
The Ultra chip combines two Max chips on one large chip using Apple’s UltraFusion architecture, so they offer double the CPU and GPU resources, and even higher memory capacity and bandwidth. It’s suited to complex 3D rendering, large AI models and scientific computing. 
M5 Max: We are already familiar with the M5 Max from the MacBook Pro that launched in March 2026. It offers an 18-core CPU and up to 40-core GPU, versus up to 16 CPU cores in the M4 Max. Its GPU includes a Neural Accelerator in every core, helping deliver up to 3.9x faster AI performance than M4 Max, according to Apple, alongside third-generation ray tracing. 
M5 Ultra: The M5 Ultra is a brand new chip that connects two dual-die M5 Max chips using UltraFusion, creating a four-die architecture and offerering up to a 36-core CPU and 80-core GPU. Apple claims up to 1.3x faster CPU, to 40% faster graphics and 4.5× peak GPU compute for AI versus M3 Ultra.


						

							




Mac Studio M5 Max benchmarks
We have tested the Mac Studio M5 Max with 18-core CPU, 40-core GPU, 128GB memory and 4TB SSD, here are the benchmarks for that model. Read our full review of the Mac Studio (M5 Max).


TestM5 Max StudioM4 Max StudioImprovement

Geekbench 7 single-core3,7823,5028%
Geekbench 7 multicore35,65829,06723%
Cinebench 2024 GPU22,43816,86633%
iMovie 4K ProRes export28 seconds31 seconds10% less time

 






Storage 
Maximum storage remains 8TB for the M5 Max and 16TB for the M5 Ultra, so capacity hasn’t increased.
However, Apple says its next-generation SSD architecture, based on PCIe Gen 6, delivers up to twice the storage performance.
Our testing of the M5 Max Mac Studio with a 4TB SSD showed substantial improvements over the tested M4 Max Studio:
2.67× the read throughput.
2.18× the write throughput.
These results apply to the tested configurations; performance may vary with SSD capacity. Faster storage could reduce the time spent opening large projects, transferring files and loading large local AI models, although the improvement will depend on your workload and any other bottlenecks. 


						

							


RAM
Maximum unified memory remains 128GB with M5 Max and 512GB with M5 Ultra, the same as the previous generation. 
Bandwidth has improved though. The M5 Max will now reach 614GB/s with the 40-core GPU configuration, up from 546GB/s on the 40-core GPU M4 Max, while M5 Ultra delivers 1.2TB/s, which Apple says is around 50 percent higher than M3 Ultra.


						

							


Connectivity: WiFi & Bluetooth
Other upgrades include Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, USB-C genlock and Thunderbolt 5 clustering for distributed AI workloads. Display support also improves, with M5 Max supporting up to five external displays and M5 Ultra supporting up to eight, depending on resolution and refresh rate.

				
					

				
			
Eugen Wegmann




Wi-Fi: The Mac Studio now supports Wi-Fi 7 which replaces the previous wireless standard Wi-Fi 6E.
Bluetooth: Bluetooth 6 replaces Bluetooth 5.3.
Ethernet: Existing connectivity including 10Gb Ethernet, HDMI, USB-A, SDXC and a headphone jack remains.
Thunderbolt: Thunderbolt 5 remains, offering up to 120Gb/s and as many as six Thunderbolt 5 ports depending on configuration. Thunderbolt 5 can now be used with RDMA to cluster multiple Mac Studios for distributed AI workloads; Apple says four systems can deliver up to 3x faster AI inference than one. 
Genlock: Apple has added Genlock support over USB-C. This is used for synchronising a display and camera (which can be an iPhone 17 Pro) and will be useful for professional video workflows.
Display support: The Mac Studio with M5 Max supports up to five external displays. The M5 Ultra supports up to eight displays at 6K/60Hz, or up to four displays at 5K/120Hz.
Other ports include two USB-C ports and an SDXC card slot on the front of the M5 Max model, and two Thunderbolt 5 ports and an SDXC card slot on the front of the M5 Ultra model. On the back of the Mac Studio are:
4× Thunderbolt 5 ports
2× USB-A ports
1× HDMI port
1× 10Gb Ethernet port
1× 3.5mm headphone jack


						

							




Mac Studio M5 Max vs M4 Max: What’s Changed

Max RAM512GB512GB

 






Who is the Mac Studio best for?
Apple has designed the Mac Studio with M5 Max to meet the needs of demanding creative and technical professionals. Apple specifically highlights musicians, photographers, software developers, designers and 3D professionals. It’s also well suited to video editing, code compilation, AI image generation and running sizeable LLMs locally.
The Mac Studio with M5 Ultra is intended for professionals with exceptionally demanding workloads: VFX artists rendering complex scenes, filmmakers working with multiple streams of 8K video, engineers running simulations, and AI researchers or data scientists training and running huge models locally. Its 512GB memory ceiling is particularly valuable for frontier-class LLMs.


						

							


Should you buy the 2026 Mac Studio?
For new buyers, the M5 Max Mac Studio is an excellent starting point. Pay extra for M5 Ultra only if your workload needs its additional resources.
Existing M4 Max owners should weigh an upgrade carefully. Our video tests showed relatively modest time savings, although workflows limited by internal storage speed may benefit more substantially. 
M3 Ultra owners shouldn’t assume M5 Max is faster across the board: it wins Cinebench GPU rendering, but M3 Ultra retains advantages in multicore rendering and Metal compute. Upgrade only if the benefits justify the cost for your work.
Availability may become limited due to the global RAM shortages. For more guidance, read: Should you buy a Mac Studio now or wait?
Considering an alternative? Read our Best Mac buying guide.

title: Apple Still Working on Anti-Snatching Feature That Locks Stolen iPhones
content:
New references in the latest iOS 27.2 beta show that Apple continues to develop a new feature which will lock your iPhone if it's snatched from your hand by a thief. 


As previously reported, the feature will use the gyroscope, accelerometer, and other sensors to determine when an iPhone has been grabbed. It'll also rely on a paired Apple Watch to detect when the iPhone has suddenly moved away from the owner's wrist. 

9to5Mac, the feature is called "AutoLock" internally, and it can use several different methods to determine whether an iPhone has been snatched from its owner:
A sharp acceleration consistent with the phone being snatched.

A paired Apple Watch remaining unreachable for a certain period.

Loss of connectivity to a paired Apple Watch.

Prolonged loss of network connectivity.

The device remaining unlocked beyond a certain interval.
There are also references to safeguards to prevent false positives, like as successful biometric authentication, or foreground app activities that could be mistakenly taken as a sign that the iPhone has been snatched.

Additional code also suggests the feature works using a voting system where a potential theft signal can request a lock, while safeguards such as biometrics and familiar locations can veto it.

When the iPhone is yanked from the owner's hand, assuming a successful theft signal, the device will lock and activate Stolen Device Protection to prevent thieves from accessing information on it.

Stolen Device Protection adds extra security to your iPhone when you're away from familiar locations like home or work. It requires biometric authentication for actions like accessing stored passwords or credit cards, and there are built-in hour-long delays for actions like changing an Apple Account password.

title: Mac mini (M5 Pro) review: Killer performance at a lethal price
content:
Macworld





At a glance
Expert's Rating



Pros
Small and quiet
Great performance for its size
Large unified memory is great for AI
Cons
The price is moving in the wrong direction
Upgrade prices are crazy as ever
Our Verdict 
Some things are objectively good, but still very hard to recommend. That’s how I feel about the Mac mini with M5 Pro. It delivers the performance improvement we expect to see two years after the prior model, but the price has gone up by even more than the performance. And Apple hasn’t made changes to the design or features to offset the plain simple fact that the value proposition—already a tough sell—has gotten worse.
Price When Reviewed

It has been almost two years since Apple introduced the Mac mini with M4 and M4 Pro. Its replacement splits generations in an odd way: the less expensive model makes the leap to M6, while the higher-endl model gets an M5 Pro, rather than an M6 Pro. For all we know, there may never be an M6 Pro.
In the time between releases, due in part to the exploding costs of RAM and flash storage as the result of a race to build AI data centers, the Mac mini jumped up significantly in price. The M6 entry-level model costs a whopping $899, a full 50 percent more than the M4’s $599 starting price, and that still includes the same 16GB of RAM and 256GB of storage.
Two years ago, we loved the power and efficiency of Apple’s surprisingly small computer, but were dismayed by how much more you paid for even the most modest upgrades. This year’s model is the same computer with a faster chip, and the price has gone through the roof. Is it still a worthwhile purchase? Let’s dive in.
M5 Pro Mac mini: Preposterous pricing
The M4 Mac mini cost $599 in late 2024, with 16GB of RAM and 256GB of storage. It was a great starting price, but at the time we noted the greedy pricing of RAM and SSD upgrades: simply stepping up one level to 32GB and 512GB of storage cost another $600. In other words, Apple was charging as much for 16GB of RAM and 256GB of storage as an upgrade as it was for an entire computer with that same RAM and storage. Absurd!
It gives me no pleasure to say that pricing has gotten much worse. The starting price of this generation, the M6 Mac mini, is 50 percent higher at $899. It still has 16GB of RAM and a 256GB SSD. It still costs $600 to add another 16GB of RAM (a total of 32GB) and 256GB of storage (a total of 512GB).
Want the more powerful chip? The M5 Pro version, with a cut-back version of the chip that has fewer CPU and GPU cores, 24GB of RAM and a 512GB SSD, is $1,699. The same configuration of the M4 Pro model was $1,399.  Basically, you’re paying $300 more to get your foot in the door with the Mac mini, a change that undermines its entire existence as a small and affordable Mac.
The version we’re reviewing here has the full M5 Pro chip (a +$200 upgrade), 48GB of RAM (+$600) an 1TB SSD (+$300), and 10 gigabit Ethernet (+$100). That’s $2,899. Two years ago, the M4 Pro version of this computer with these same specs cost $2,299, and even that felt high.
For reference, the Mac Studio with M5 Max (18-core CPU and 32-core GPU), 36GB of RAM, and a 1TB SSD is actually less expensive at $2,799, offers more ports, and has a much more powerful GPU.
I know the prices of all things related to computers have gone crazy lately, but this is just ridiculous and shows how disproportionate Apple’s upgrade pricing has gotten. Make it make sense, Apple.
M5 Pro Mac mini: Design
Physically, the new Mac mini is exactly like the two-year-old model. It has exactly the same dimensions, weight, and port configuration, including three Thunderbolt 5 ports on the back and two USB-C ports in the front.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




There are three small improvements worth noting, other than the obvious jump from the M4/M4 Pro to the M6/M5 Pro:
The Ethernet port is a 2.5 gigabit port, rather than a gigabit port (you can still opt for a 10 gigabit port).
It uses Apple’s N1 wireless chip, so you get Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 (up from Wi-FI 6E and Bluetooth 5.3).
The Thunderbolt 5 ports support higher resolutions and refresh rates when using multiple connected displays.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The bottom still has the same round ventilation riser and a recessed power button that is, for better or worse, rather hard to get to.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




M5 Pro Mac mini: Performance
After two years, what you’re really paying hundreds of dollars more for is the new chip. While the M6 is the newest generation, there are no higher-end “Pro” or “Max” versions of it. Instead, the higher-end Mac mini is the same M5 Pro introduced in the MacBook Pro about six months ago.
It’s quite a bit faster than the M4 Pro was, but we had reservations about the price/performance ratio on that computer and those have only gotten worse now. As time goes on, computers are supposed to get more powerful at the same price, or even cheaper. They’re not supposed to be 25 percent faster but cost 30% more. And yet here we are.
Geekbench 7
Let’s take a look at CPU and GPU compute performance with the latest edition of the ever-reliable Geekbench.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




That’s a 12 percent jump in single-core CPU performance over the M4 Pro from 2 years ago, and a bigger 38 percent jump in multi-core performance. We went form 14 cores (10 performance and 4 efficiency) to 18 cores (6 super and 12 performance), hence the big boost in multi-threaded CPU performance.
Let’s look at GPU compute power for the M5 Pro, which has the same 20 GPU cores as the M4 Pro.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




We’re looking at an improvement of around 20 percent for the GPU, partly from the higher-performing GPU cores and partly from the extra 12 percent of memory bandwidth.
Geekbench AI
AI performance is becoming increasingly important. Even if you’re not a big user of local AI agents, Apple’s own machine learning tools are prevalent throughout the system, from Siri AI to Photos to Dictation and so much more. The Geekbench AI test lets you run a series of common ML tasks using the CPU, GPU, or Neural Engine. We’re interested in the latter’s performance here.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Neural Engine performance keeps creeping upward, from the M4 Pro to M5 to M5 Pro. It’s about 33 percent faster in the low-precision data formats that are most often used when you’re not doing AI training.
We don’t have data for the M6 Mac mini yet, but this is one area where that much less expensive system could outstrip the M5 Pro model, possibly by a wide margin. With the Neural Engine doubled to 32 cores, we can expect lower-precision AI tasks where memory bandwidth isn’t the limit to run a lot faster.
Cinebench 2026
Cinebench is a great test of a certain kind of CPU performance as it renders “offline” computer graphics, the kind of high-quality but very slow rendering used in TV and film.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




A single core is only 11 percent faster, but when they’re all working at once, the higher core count and change to the core configuration in the M5 Pro make a big difference. Performance goes up by 40 percent, a big jump even when you consider its has been two years between products.
HandBrake video encode
HandBrake uses standard video encoder libraries to transcode videos. We used the Creative Commons license Tears of Steel video in 4K, and transcode it down to a 1080p H.265 format, using both a CPU-based x265 encoder and the “videotoolbox” encoder that leverages Apple’s dedicated video encoding hardware.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




This test is a measure of how many seconds the transcode takes, so shorter results are better. Again, the increase in core count and configuration change results in a big multi-core CPU benefit, as the CPU-based encoder runs 26 percent faster. The newer hardware video encoder gets even a bigger boost, though—it’s done in 41 percent less time!
Game benchmarks
A Mac mini is not really a gamer’s machine. You’d be crazy to spend this kind of money on a Mac expecting to play the latest games, and the limited cooling potential of a little Mac mini enclosure makes it struggle and get loud when playing a high-end game. Still, game benchmarks tend to stress the entire system at once—the CPU, GPU, and memory—and are a great look at total system performance.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The Borderlands 3 test only runs a little faster at lower resolutions and settings. But Apple’s newer GPU, despite still only having 20 cores, runs the game much better at 4K and High settings. You get a 52 percent improvement with those particular settings, though it’s still not really very smooth, and we would recommend lower settings for anyone trying to play this on a Mac mini.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The real-time strategy game Total War: Warhammer III is very demanding, and at 4K the M5 Pro just can’t cut it. There’s still a 31 percent improvement at 1080p and High settings, however.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Rise of the Tomb Raider is getting a little old, and most modern Macs can run it quite well. The new Mac mini runs this game about 10-15 percent better than the one from two years ago.
Overall, the combination of more CPU cores in a higher-performing configuration, a bit more memory bandwidth, and a new GPU core design pays off for 3D games. 
Blackmagic Disk Speed
A final bit of great news as we close out the benchmarks. Apple’s latest SSD hardware is fully present here, offering a huge boost to performance where it was sorely needed. 

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Back in the M1 and M2 days, Apple’s storage performance was second to none. But as you can see, it remained stagnant for years, and only recently doubled in performance with the latest generation. This puts it back on the level with some of the best Windows PCs you can buy. 
Should you buy an M5 Pro Mac mini?
There’s not much to talk about with the new M5 Pro Mac mini other than performance. It looks identical to the 2-year-old model that preceded it, and have only modest improvements to wireless features and multi-display support that most users will probably not notice. So what we have, essentially, is the same computer as Apple was selling in late 2024, only faster.
The good news is, it’s an appropriate speed boost given the two year gap. A CPU speedup of 10-30 percent and a GPU improvement of 20-40 percent is what you can expect in most cases, which would be a lot for a year-over-year boost, but is about what we expect after two years between releases. It’s a respectable improvement. If the price was the same, we could confidently claim this is a very good update.
But the price is not the same. Two years ago, the base model of the Mac mini was a very good deal, but the value proposition quickly disintegrated when you started adding on Apple’s outrageously-priced upgrades.
Today, the base model is 50 percent more expensive and higher configurations cost hundreds of dollars more. The model I reviewed two years ago was $2,299 and configured almost exactly like the one I’m reviewing now, save for the M5 Pro instead of the M4 Pro. Now it costs you $2,899.
That’s not how it’s supposed to work. As time marches on, you’re supposed to get a faster computer for the same price or less. Or at least a bunch of new features to make up the difference. An identical machine that is 25-30 percent faster but costs 25-50 percent more is moving in the wrong direction. Of course, the current RAM and SSD crunch are affecting everyone, and every company writing a blank check for endless AI investment is to blame. The price increases that resulted from this are not Apple’s fault, but it is Apple’s problem.
This is a good computer at a bad price, and it’s not worth the upgrade if you’re not in desperate need of one. And if you are, I feel sorry for you; this is a terrible time to buy any computer.

title: Apple is doomed because there aren’t enough iPhones to buy
content:
Macworld





You feel it, too, right? That sense that things have changed. Our long-held traditions are about to be upended. Where it will lead, no one can say. All we know is that it is happening and there is no going back.
No, the Macalope isn’t talking about John Ternus taking over as Apple CEO, although that’s also looming large over the Apple world currently. No, he’s talking about the company flipping the table on the iPhone release schedule.
It’s not the first time Apple’s mixed it up, of course. If you’re old enough to remember when people still thought the last season of “Lost” was going to tie up all the loose ends, you will recall that the new iPhones used to be released in the summer. “Don’t wear linen and don’t use last year’s iPhone after Labor Day,” people used to say. (No one said that.) But with the release of the iPhone 4S, Apple switched to a fall schedule in order to ruin the summer plans of its engineers and product marketing employees.
Now, after 15 years of relative stability, Apple has completely bifurcated its iPhone release, moving the release of the base iPhone models and the iPhone Air to the spring along with the iPhone e-line. Further, for those who weren’t happy just paying in the $1,000 range for iPhones, the company added the iPhone Duo, creating an exciting new range of $2,000 options. Just what everyone was begging for in our current era of $6 per gallon gas and $26 salad entrees.
Nothing against the iPhone Duo; it looks like a fantastic phone, but the Macalope could really go for an iPhone 5c right now.
After years of a reliable cycle of iPhone releases and then inevitable rumors of drastic production cuts that supposedly mean this year’s line of iPhones is a huge failure instead of them being absolutely normal decreases after the fall surge, the horny one isn’t sure what to expect. First of all, the overall number of units sold will be down drastically since there’s no base model this quarter, plus the five people who bought the iPhone Air. Additionally, the introduction of the iPhone Duo means many who would have bought the iPhone 18 Pro will not. 
Indeed, the headlines are already rolling in: “iPhone 18 Pro Pre-Orders Off to a Muted Start, Analyst Says”
Of course, Apple wants the iPhone Duo to be a hit, and it knew that would come at the cost of iPhone Pro sales. In fact, in order to grease the skids for the Touch ID-only iPhone Duo even further, Apple even put a bug in Face ID on the iPhone 18 Pro to even the playing field.

				
					

				
			
If you’d like to receive regular news and updates to your inbox, sign up for our newsletters, including The Macalope and Apple Breakfast, David Price’s weekly, bite-sized roundup of all the latest Apple news and rumors.

Foundry




Verrry clever, Apple. Well done. But the Macalope sees you.
The horny one has made great hay over the years by sinking his antlers into the annual pearl-clutching over iPhone production cuts, so he’s eager to see what analysts will have to say this year. Added to the fact that the iPhone Duo is likely not to sell in high numbers anyway because of its relatively high price, you can expect Apple reporting to look like a back alley in Gotham City after a showing of “The Mark of Zorro”. Just pearls everywhere.
Production cut fever hit its deafening crescendo with the release of the iPhone X in 2017. The iPhone X was rumored to have had massive production cuts that never made any sense, and the phone was ultimately revealed to have been a big success. Will we get Product Cut Fever 2.0 this year?! Very exciting!
Then we have the spring, when a young person’s fancy turns to… uh, cheap phones, hopefully, because that’s what we’re getting, and a new iPhone Air. One of Tim Cook’s major legacies as CEO was smoothing revenue until it became an almost completely frictionless surface. A rollout of the expensive phones in the fall and the cheaper phones in the spring will certainly aid in that effort. Only Apple really knows how much iPhone buying in the latter part of the year is for the holidays, but moving a large chunk of the product rollout to the spring may reduce the urgency and FOMO of the purchasing decision. People will still buy the same number of phones most likely, but they may not buy them on launch day in the numbers they do in the fall.
Apple easily navigated the previous change in iPhone release, and the Macalope expects it will do so again. The only question is how well analysts handle it.

title: Apple Music Hall Spatial Audio Venue Opens in Battersea Power Station
content:
Apple has announced the opening of Apple Music Hall, a state-of-the-art 600-capacity music venue located in London's Battersea Power Station. Apple says it is "designed to connect artists and fans through bespoke, intimate performances unlike anywhere else."


Apple says the hall incorporates heritage brickwork, fluted arches, and bronze balconies reminiscent of the historic oriel windows, while a giant glass wall "further enhances the visual connection with the historic building, offering a panoramic view of the concourse and the river beyond."

The 38-foot-wide stage can be reconfigured for traditional front-facing sets or more in-the-round experiences, and a 48-speaker spatial sound system is positioned all around the audience. Behind the stage is a dedicated recording and mix studio so that every performance can be captured as a multi-track recording and mixed in Spatial Audio, live or in post-production.


The venue is also hardwired for 16 or more cameras that feed a purpose-built broadcast control room with infrastructure that supports iPhone video capture running in parallel alongside traditional broadcast cameras.

The exhaustive setup means artists can perform a live show, record it in Spatial Audio, create a broadcast-ready mix, and capture multicamera video – all directly in the venue.


Apple says performances out of Apple Music Hall will also be livestreamed globally so fans outside of London can tune in to enjoy shows from their favorite artists. For more information about Apple Music Hall, including tickets for upcoming shows, fans can visit applemusichall.com or follow @applemusichall on Instagram and TikTok.

title: Apple CEO John Ternus Talks iPhone Duo Design, Siri AI, and Becoming CEO
content:
Apple CEO John Ternus did an interview with Canal+ talk show Clique following Apple's September event. He discussed the iPhone Duo's design, difficulties Apple ran into when developing it, his plans for Apple, and more.



On the design of the ‌iPhone Duo‌, Ternus explained why Apple went with an iPad-like shape when the device is unfolded.
I think it's something new and unique, right? But I think we didn't want to just do what we'd seen other people do, which is sort of take two phone shapes and stick them together and then you get this weird square thing. We came at it from we want to build a large screen experience that feels right to us. And obviously we've been doing that for a long time with iPad. And so we knew kind of the shape, you know, we came up with this new aspect ratio.

Ternus said that when developing the ‌iPhone Duo‌, there were "so many problems" to solve, but a foldable was an opportunity for Apple employees to "be really clever" and "come up with entirely new things." He said some of the hardware engineering problems Apple had to address involved the design of the hinge and the display, and making them reliable.

When asked to share his favorite ‌iPhone Duo‌ trick, Ternus showed off the device's opening animation. "I mean, this is really fun, you know, the animation that you get as you open it across from one side to the other. It's just sort of whimsical and fun. And it brings a smile to your face."

Siri AI is "not designed to be your friend," which is something we heard earlier this year from Craig Federighi. Ternus said Apple doesn't want to replace human relationships. "They're how we learn, they're how we grow, they're how we find joy and happiness," he said.

Tim Cook and Apple's board asked Ternus if he wanted to be the next Apple CEO. Ternus didn't say when he was approached, but he said the question came as a surprise. "When Tim asked me if it was something I would consider, I would say the good news is I was sitting down, because I never in a million years would have imagined that happening," said Ternus.

As Apple's CEO, Ternus said he doesn't have plans for a radical change. He was asked if Apple was going back to its roots under his leadership, with more of a focus on engineering products.
I don't think anything's really changed. Sure, I'm new in this job, but the focus on innovation, the focus on products, the focus most importantly on our customers, that has never changed. That's been here from the beginning.


Ternus said it was "amazing" to be able to say "one more thing" on stage at Apple's September event. "I've seen Steve say it, and I've seen Tim say it," he said. "And so having the opportunity for me to say it was pretty magical. Kind of goosebumps."

full interview includes Ternus' thoughts on ‌Tim Cook‌, the AI race, Apple's environmental goals, the Vision Pro, the new parental controls added in iOS 27, and more.

title: Latest macOS beta: What’s new and should you install it?
content:
Macworld





Apple released macOS 27 Golden Gate on September 14, 2026, but development hasn’t stopped. Just two days later on September 16, Apple issued the first developer beta of macOS 27.2, beginning testing of the operating system’s next major point update. Yes, that’s macOS 27.2, not macOS 27.1. 
The macOS 27.2 beta gives developers and testers early access to Apple’s latest fixes, refinements and any features that weren’t ready for the initial Golden Gate release. 
However, as with any beta software, it may introduce bugs, compatibility problems and poorer battery life so we recommend caution if you wish to install it.
Here’s everything you need to know about the latest macOS beta, including what’s new, when the next public beta is likely to arrive and whether you should install it.


What’s the latest macOS beta? 
Apple offers two beta streams: a developer beta and a public beta. The public beta allows enthusiasts and early adopters to test upcoming changes before they are released to everyone. You need to join Apple’s Beta Software Program to access it.
The latest Mac beta is macOS 27.2 beta 2, which Apple released to registered developers on September 21, 2026. It arrived less than a weekbeta 1.
The corresponding macOS 27.2 public beta is expected shortly. Public betas usually follow developer betas, although Apple does not guarantee a particular schedule.
macOS 27 Golden Gate beta version tracker 
Apple released macOS 27.2 Golden Gate Developer Beta 2 on September 21, 2026.
The macOS 27.2 Golden Gate Public Beta 2 should be released sometime the same week; new versions are usually released a day or two after the new developer beta.
macOS 26 Tahoe beta: Apple may continue updating macOS 26 Tahoe with security and maintenance releases, but macOS 27 is now the current operating system and the focus of Apple’s beta program.


						

							




macOS 27 Beta timeline


ReleaseDate
Beta 1June 8, 2026
Beta 2June 22, 2026
Beta 3July 6, 2026
Beta 3 v.2July 13, 2026
Beta 4July 20, 2026
Beta 5August 10, 2026
Beta 6August 17, 2026
Beta 7August 24, 2026
Beta 8August 31, 2026
Release Candidate 1September 9, 2026
Public Beta 1July 13, 2026
Public Beta 2July 22, 2026
Public Beta 3August 11, 2026
Public Beta 4August 17, 2026
Public Beta 5August 24, 2026
Public Beta 6August 31, 2026
Final ReleaseSeptember 14, 2026
macOS 27.2 developer beta 1September 16, 2026
macOS 27.2 developer beta 2September 21, 2026

 






What’s new in the latest beta?

				
					

				
			
New features in macOS 27.

Foundry




Apple has not announced any major consumer-facing additions in macOS 27.2 beta 2. The following changes are expected though:
Bug fixes and performance improvements: Addressing issues in the first release of macOS 27.
Additional Siri AI languages: Apple has said the Siri AI will expand to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish in October. 
Automatic password changes: The promised feature that automatically changes compromised passwords has not yet been implemented, but it could arrive in macOS 27.2.. 
We’ll update this section as changes are discovered.
See Apple’s developer website for more information about the beta. 


						

							


Should you install the macOS beta?

				
					

				
			
Apple




Installing the macOS beta lets you test Apple’s next round of features, fixes and refinements before their public release. Most Mac users should remain on the standard version of macOS 27, particularly if they rely on their Mac for work.
Install if…
You need to test apps
You want early access to new features
You have a secondary Mac available
Wait if…
This is your primary work machine
You rely on niche or specialist software
Stability is critical to your workflow


						

							






Who are you Should you install?

A developer testing appsConsider the developer beta
An enthusiast with a spare MacConsider the public beta 
General user with one MacStay on macOS 27

 






What are the risks of installing beta software?
Installing pre-release software on a primary device carries several risks.
System instability: Performance problems, freezes, crashes, and other unexpected behavior are common during beta testing.
App failures: Third-party applications may crash, behave unpredictably, or stop working entirely.
Hardware strain: Early beta builds can increase battery drain and cause Macs to run hotter than usual.
Data loss: Software bugs may corrupt files, and downgrading to a stable version often requires a complete system reset.


						

							


Safety precautions and best practices
If you decide to install the beta, take the following precautions:
Use a secondary device: Avoid installing beta software on your primary Mac or on any machine used for critical work.
Create a full backup: Use Time Machine to create a complete backup before upgrading so you can restore your Mac if something goes wrong. Note that this needs to be a Time Machine backup from before the beta was installed and you will lose anything saved subsequently.
Install on a separate volume: Consider installing the beta on a separate volume or external SSD rather than replacing your main operating system.
Check storage space: Make sure you have at least 15GB of free storage available before beginning the installation.


						

							


How to install the macOS beta

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The process for installing a macOS beta depends on whether you are seeking the Developer Beta or the Public Beta. Apple simplified this process a few years ago, removing the need for a paid developer account to access early builds. 
The first step is to join Apple’s beta testing program. We explain how to do that in a separate article.
You will need to register your account either as a public beta tester or as a developer in order to enable beta updates on your Mac.
To install the beta follow these steps:
Back up your Mac: Before installing any pre-release software, it is critical to prepare your Mac to avoid data loss. Beta software is inherently unstable and can cause crashes or app compatibility issues. 
Register your account either as a public beta tester or as a developer in order to enable beta updates on your Mac:
For the Public Beta: Visit the Apple Beta Software Program website, sign in with your Apple ID, and agree to the terms.
For the Developer Beta: Register as an Apple Developer on Apple’s website, download the Apple Developer app from the App Store, sign in with your standard Apple ID, and complete the free registration process.
On the Mac where you wish to install the beta, open System Settings and navigate to General > Software Update.
Click the (i) info button next to Beta Updates.
Enable Beta Updates.
The beta will appear as an available upgrade. Select the macOS beta you want to install (e.g., macOS Public Beta or Developer Beta).
Click Upgrade Now to begin the download and installation.
As long as you are a registered developer or enrolled in the public beta program, when the relevant macOS Beta becomes available, it will also show up on your Mac.
Once you are running the beta, the updates will come through to your Mac automatically; you just need to go to Software Update in System Settings and click to install. See How to install macOS.


						

							


How to get a free Apple developer account
If you just want a free Apple Developer account so you can access the beta, you can get this via Xcode or the Apple Developer app in iOS. Here’s how to do it via the Apple Developer app on an iPhone:
Get the Apple Developer App from the App Store. 
Open the app on your iPhone. 
Tap on Account. 
Tap on Sign In. 
Sign in using your usual Apple ID. 
If you wish to actually publish applications to the App Store or receive support, you’ll need to pay $99/£79 per year for a paid account. You can compare the free and paid accounts here.


						

							





 FAQ 


1.
Who can run the macOS beta?
Anyone can run the macOS beta, but to do so, you do need to register for either the developer beta, the public beta, or both.
Apple offers both developer and public beta programs for macOS, enabling all interested users to test pre-release versions of the operating system. While both betas provide early access to new features, they cater to different user profiles based on technical expertise and risk tolerance. Beta software tends to be buggy so the more stable public beta version may be preferable, but even that will not be bug-free.
In the past, the developer beta was only available to developers who had paid to join Apple’s Developer Program (which costs $99/£79). However, for a couple of years now, Apple has opened up the developer beta to registered developers with free developer accounts. We explain how to get a free developer account below. 
If you decide you no longer want to run the beta version of macOS read this: How to remove the macOS beta.





2.
macOS public beta vs developer beta
Since 2023, the Developer Beta has been available to anyone who registers as a developer, even if they aren’t a paid-up member of Apple’s Developer Program. As a result, people with a basic free developer account can download the new macOS developer beta (we show you how to register below).
Whether you should download the developer beta if you aren’t a developer is another question. We don’t recommend you install the developer beta if you aren’t a developer. Instead, our recommendation is to use the public beta (the first version of which usually arrives in July).
There are a few differences between the public and developer betas. The public beta is not the same as the beta that is released through the developer program. The public beta typically launches after the developer beta has undergone initial testing and refinement
Developers get updates to their beta first, and possibly more frequently. But you should keep in mind that betas are by nature not stable, and because the public beta comes after the developer beta it could be a little safer to install. 
The most significant difference is probably the motive of the testers: Developers usually have the aim of ensuring their apps work when the updated macOS is released to the general public, while public beta testers are essentially helping Apple detect bugs and offering feedback on the features. Because of this, developers may get to test new features not available in the public beta. 
If you want to get the public beta the first thing you need to do, if you haven’t already, is join Apple’s beta programs read this for more information: How to become an Apple beta tester.





3.
Is the macOS beta stable?
By its nature, a beta has the potential to be unstable. Therefore, it’s not advised that you install it on a Mac that you rely on. If you have a second Mac that isn’t mission-critical, then install it there. We strongly recommend that you don’t risk all by putting the macOS beta on your primary Mac, especially not in the early days of the beta development. 
If you don’t have a second Mac, there are a couple of ways you could run macOS beta on your Mac without running the risk of losing data or finding your Mac stops working:
We recommend installing it on a partition, which these days is really a volume (and is much easier to create than a partition was). Read about how to do that here: How to dual-boot Mac: Run two versions of macOS on a Mac.
Alternatively, you could install the macOS beta on an external drive and run it on that.
We discuss the safety of the macOS beta and the risks you might be taking in more detail in a separate article.





4.
How to prepare your Mac for the beta
Update your software: We recommend you have the latest full version of macOS installed, although Apple says that the macOS Developer Beta Access Utility requires macOS 10.8 or later.
Make space: We’d recommend at least 25-30GB of available space because the macOS betas tend to be very large. If you end up requiring more space, read: How to free up space on Mac. Note that we always recommend that you have at least 10% space free on your Mac at any time, so if you don’t have that, expect problems!
Back up: Before you install a beta on your Mac, you should make a backup of your data and files. You can find out how to use Time Machine to back up your Mac. We also have a round-up of suitable backup solutions.





5.
How to send feedback to Apple
Should you come across an error or a bug, you should use the Feedback Assistant app to provide feedback to Apple. Launch the app and follow the appropriate steps, selecting the area about which you’re providing feedback and then any specific sub-area. Then describe your issue in a single sentence, before providing a more detailed description, including any specific steps that reproduce the issue. You’ll also be able to attach other files.
You’ll also have to give permission for the Feedback Assistant app to collect diagnostic information from your Mac.
It won’t always be obvious whether something is a bug or just not as easy to use as you might have hoped. Either way, if your feedback is that something appears to work in an illogical way, Apple will want to know that.
If you are having trouble with a third-party app, you can let Apple know by reporting it through the 3rd-party Application Compatibility category in the Feedback Assistant. However, we’d suggest that you also provide feedback to the app’s developer, who will no doubt be grateful.





6.
Will I be able to update from macOS beta to the final version?
Beta users can move to the finished release once its build is newer than – or equivalent to – the beta installed. Read: How to leave the macOS beta.  





7.
Can I talk about the beta publicly?
According to Apple and the license agreement all beta testers must agree to, the beta is “Apple confidential information”. By accepting those terms, you agree not to discuss your use of the software with anyone who isn’t also in the Beta Software Program. That means you can’t “blog, post screenshots, tweet, or publicly post information about the public beta software.”
However, you can discuss any information that Apple has publicly disclosed; the company says that information is no longer considered confidential.





8.
How to downgrade from the macOS beta
You can always revert to an earlier version of macOS, though depending on how you back up, it’s not necessarily a painless process.
Start by making sure the data on your drive is backed up, then erase the drive and install the latest public version of macOS. When you first start up your Mac, you can use the Migration Assistant to import your data from the backup. Here’s a more detailed tutorial on downgrading from the macOS beta and we also have a tutorial on downgrading to an older version of the Mac OS.





9.
Is the beta free to download? 
Yes, the macOS beta is free to download for both developers and the general public. Apple offers two distinct tracks for testing pre-release software: the Developer Beta and the Public Beta, both of which are now accessible without a paid subscription.





10.
Can I go back to the stable version?
Yes, you can go back to the stable version of macOS from a beta, but the complexity of the process depends on whether the final version of that software has been released yet.
If you are running macOS 27.2 beta and want to return to the current public release of macOS 27, simply turning off Beta Updates will stop future beta installations, but it will not immediately downgrade the Mac. To return before Apple releases an equivalent public build, you may need to erase the Mac and reinstall macOS, then restore data from a backup made before installing the beta.





11.
Should I install the beta on my main Mac?
Installing a macOS beta on your primary computer is generally not recommended due to the inherent risks of using unfinished software. While beta programs offer early access to new features, they are designed for testing and often contain significant bugs that can disrupt your daily workflow.





12.
Do I need an Apple Developer account to install the beta?
You do not need a paid Apple Developer account to install the macOS beta. While access to developer betas was previously restricted to those paying a $99/£79 annual fee, Apple changed this policy in 2023 to allow anyone with a free developer account to access these builds. Alternatively, you can join the Public Beta program, which is also free and accessible to anyone with a valid Apple ID.





13.
How often are new beta versions released?
New macOS beta versions are typically released every one to two weeks, with the frequency increasing as the final public release date approaches. The beta updates refine features and address bugs identified by testers.





14.
Is the macOS beta safe to install?
The beta is generally safe to test, but it may contain bugs that cause crashes, poor battery life, app compatibility issues, or data loss. Always back up your Mac before installing.





15.
Will my apps work with the macOS beta?
Many apps will work normally, but some third-party software may crash, perform poorly, or not launch at all until developers release updates.

title: GM Wants You to Know It Still Plans to Ditch Apple CarPlay in Future EVs
content:
Recent reports claiming that General Motors is reversing course on its controversial plans to ditch CarPlay in its future EVs appear to be incorrect.


As noted by Joanna Stern, host of the YouTube channel New Things, a GM spokesperson has confirmed that its new software interface that shows CarPlay or Android Auto alongside its own native system in 2027 models of its Chevrolet Silverado and GMC Sierra is specific to the gas-powered versions of those pickup trucks.

GM previously stated that CarPlay and Android Auto would continue to be offered in its new gas-powered vehicles for the "foreseeable future," so the 2027 models of those trucks still supporting those platforms is not a change of course.

There is one more wrinkle in that GM's all-electric 2027 Cadillac LYRIQ supports CarPlay and Android Auto still — it is unclear if the Lyriq will always be an exception or if it will simply be one of GM's final EVs to ever support phone mirroring systems. Overall, though, GM continues to insist that its future EVs will not offer CarPlay.

title: iOS 27.2 beta 2 is out now, skipping over iOS 27.1
content:
Macworld





Just a couple days after the wide release of iOS 27, Apple has released the first beta of iOS 27.2. That’s not a typo: it’s iOS 27.2, not 27.1. We never saw a 27.1 release, but Apple is beginning beta tests for the 27.2 branch.
This likely has something to do with the iPhone Duo, which is going on sale in October. We know the iPhone Duo will come with iOS 27.1, but we don’t yet know if any other devices will ever get a 27.1 update, or when all the devices will get on the same version together.
Update September 21: The second beta release is out now, less than a week after the first. 
What’s new in iOS 27.2
As beta testers report new capabilities in this version, we’ll report them here. 
New Health app: The 27.2 beta includes the new Health app, with a totally new redesign and AI-powered health insights.
Siri AI languages: Apple said that Siri AI, which launched supporting only U.S. English, will expand to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish in October.
Dual Capture for Group FaceTime: Users can stream their front and rear cameras at the same time during FaceTime calls.
Podcasts Up Next: Up Next has been refreshed with two rows at the top of the Home tab: New Episodes and Continue Playing.
Simple Profiles on iOS/iPadOS/web: The Apple TV feature that lets you use multiple different account profiles now works in the Apple TV app on iOS, iPadOS, and the web.
Multiview in Apple TV: The feature that lets you watch four select sports streams at the same time on Apple TV now works on the Apple TV app on iOS.
iOS 27.2: How to install the public beta
If you want to test the iOS 27 beta releases but are not a registered developer, follow these steps:
Click Sign Up on the Apple Beta page and register with your Apple ID.
Log in to the Beta Software Program.
Click Enroll your iOS device.
Open the Settings app, tap General, then Software Update.
In the Beta Updates section, select the iOS Public Beta.
It may take a few moments after registering for the beta option to appear in Software Update.
iOS 27.2: How to install the developer beta
You’ll need to be registered as an Apple developer, but a free developer account will do. You can get one via Xcode or the Apple Developer app in iOS. Here’s how to do it via the Apple Developer app:
Download the Apple Developer App from the App Store.
Open the app.
Tap on Account.
Sign in using your usual Apple ID.

iPhone 18 Pro Max: From $54.12 a month for 24 months via Apple Upgrade




For iPhone 14 Pro and iPhone 14 Pro Max owners considering a new device, the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ is a worthwhile upgrade. Four generations of changes bring improvements to the display, every camera on the device, battery life, charging, sustained performance, and connectivity. Battery life is likely to be the strongest improvement for most users, particularly if their current device no longer comfortably lasts through the day, while faster wired charging makes brief charging stops more useful. The newer battery is also designed to retain 80% of its original capacity for twice as many complete charge cycles under ideal conditions, and Charge Limit offers more control over long-term battery wear.

USB-C is another significant quality-of-life improvement for iPhone 14 Pro owners. It allows the iPhone to share cables with recent Macs, iPads, and accessories, while the jump from USB 2 to USB 3 speeds makes large wired photo and video transfers far quicker. The Action button and Camera Control also provide two new physical controls that the iPhone 14 Pro lacks.

The camera upgrade is especially compelling for anyone who regularly takes photos or records video. Higher-resolution Ultra Wide and Telephoto cameras expand the options beyond the Main camera, while the variable aperture and Pro controls provide additional creative flexibility. Both iPhone 14 Pro sizes move from a 3x Telephoto camera to 4x, alongside an optical-quality 8x option that substantially extends their usable reach.

Apple Vision Pro owners. The square front-camera sensor makes landscape framing easier without rotating the phone, while Center Stage improves flexibility for group photos and video calls.

The A20 Pro and vapor chamber cooling make the strongest performance case for users who play demanding games, record long video clips, or regularly push their device through sustained workloads. The increase from 6GB to 12GB of RAM and the additional AI processing hardware also enable ‌Apple Intelligence‌, ‌Siri‌ AI, and ‌Visual Intelligence‌, none of which are available on the iPhone 14 Pro. The older model still supports ‌iOS 27‌ and remains capable for messaging, browsing, photography, and other everyday activities, so the latest software update does not make it obsolete.

There are physical trade-offs to consider. Both newer models are taller and thicker, although the move from stainless steel to aluminum means the weight increases by only 5 grams on the Pro and 9 grams on the Pro Max despite the larger displays and batteries. The aluminum enclosure improves thermal management, but it is less premium-looking, and it may show dents and scratches more readily than the iPhone 14 Pro's stainless steel frame.

If your iPhone 14 Pro still meets your needs and comfortably lasts through the day, upgrading is not urgent, but you may want to think about getting a new device soon. A battery replacement may be worth considering if reduced health is your main complaint and you would otherwise be happy to keep your device. The upgrade becomes much easier to recommend when battery limitations coincide with a desire for ‌Apple Intelligence‌, USB-C, the newer cameras, and a larger display.

title: iPhone 18 Pro owners report two serious bugs causing freezes and restarts
content:
Macworld





Apple upped the price of its phones this year, and while the new iPhone 18 Pro doesn’t cost quite as much as its Max sibling (let alone the $1,999+ iPhone Duo) it’s in the premium bracket where everything needs to be perfect. And sadly, that doesn’t appear to be the case.
The 18 Pro went on sale on Friday (triggering a heartening amount of customer hype) and two bugs have already been reported.
Frozen screen bug
Alleged bug number one: in some cases and at some times, the iPhone 18 Pro’s screen is believed to stop responding to touch. One owner posted a video of this behavior to Twitter/X; their thumb appears to swipe up and down on the display (while using a social media app, possibly Twitter), yet nothing happens in response.


iPhone 18 Pro randomly stops responding to touch 😭 pic.twitter.com/xr76g6OyHc
— Noah Cat (@Cartidise) September 20, 2026





When a commenter on the post claimed that this is a bug in iOS 27 rather than the iPhone 18 Pro, and that the poster “swiped down both Notification Center and Control Center at the same time which causes the phone to freeze,” the poster responded that they didn’t “exploit any bug” and that the problem has happened twice already. Then they link to a second user reporting the same issue.
We’ve also seen a similar complaint about touch sensitivity on Reddit, although this might have a different cause; the owner mentions use of a screen protector.
Face ID bug
Alleged bug number two: a Face ID bug has caused some iPhone 18 Pro handsets to freeze and then reboot. What appears to happen is that when a Face ID verification fails, the behavior triggers.
A thread on Reddit contains the following complaint: “Not even 24 hours and I have my 18 Pro Max panic restarting. Three times due to Face ID and one by some timeout (whilst loading Apple Wallet). Called Apple support, done a Face ID reset after three restarts.”
Of the 24 direct responses from other users, 22 confirm that they’ve experienced the same or a similar issue. Some speculate (as we saw with the touch sensitivity bug) that it could be an issue with iOS 27 or other software rather than the new hardware. As evidenced by the testimony of one commenter and the original poster, the bug affects the 18 Pro Max as well as the 18 Pro.
As 9to5Mac notes in its coverage of this second bug, the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max feature a redesigned, smaller Face ID sensor array, which may be at the root of the issue. The site speculates that there may be a glitch in the section of iOS 27 which relates to this specific piece of hardware.
The original poster of the Reddit thread, however, reports that after they got in touch with Apple support, the company ran diagnostics and decided that it was a faulty unit.
Macworld can’t confirm the existence of these bugs. But these aren’t one-off complaints; multiple customers report each of the problems, which makes it unlikely that they’re imaginary. In the case of the Face ID bug, Macworld readers may be able to reproduce the behavior for themselves by attempting to unlock a protected app or document (such as a locked note in Notes) and then obscuring their face so it fails.
If these do turn out to be legitimate bugs they will join a long list of post-launch iPhone complaints, including Antennagate in 2010 and Bendgate in 2014. Last year we had Scratchgate, which didn’t go viral in the same way but caused a fuss for a while, and an issue with photos having small blacked-out portions. That second one was officially acknowledged by Apple; it remains to be seen how the company will respond to these latest reports.
creator: Macworld

title: The Glacier iPhone 18 Pro Max is the anti-Cosmic Orange
content:
Macworld





I have an iPhone 18 Pro Max. Its color finish is Glacier. And I am of a generation that uses the term “cool” as a way to show approval, even if over the years, “cool” has gone from an enthusiastic expression to a subdued feeling.
When it comes to my reaction to the Glacier iPhone 18 Pro Max, the first word I turn to is “cool.” I want to think it deserves a better word, but I can’t think of one. Glacier is cool because my reaction to it is cool, too. It’s nice, pretty, even. And though calling Glacier “cool” seems a bit on-the-nose, it fits.

				
					

				
			The cool and the hot of iPhone color theory.
Foundry




But as I said, “cool” is subdued, and that’s how I feel about it. It’s not slap-you-in-the-face, look-at-me-I-said-look-at-me like Cosmic Orange. Cosmic Orange is not cool. Cosmic Orange is hot, in a Paris Hilton way.
Oh, Cosmic Orange. How I adore Cosmic Orange. In a world where black, gray, and white dominate smartphones, Cosmic Orange stands out with pride. A flex, even–when you see it, those who know, know. 

				
					

				
			
Foundry




There’s another reason why I enjoy Cosmic Orange. It’s a callback to the fun times of the original iMac, the Bondi Blue statement that shook up technology. How dare Apple give a computer some personality! We loved it. Cosmic Orange brought that fun back.
Glacier is cool. But Cosmic Orange is a legend. It’s going to be hard for Apple to come up with another color that has the same impact.

				
					

				
			Cosmic Orange clashes with Apple’s Crisp Blue iPhone 18 Pro Max Silicone Case with MagSafe, but maybe that’s how you roll.

title: This clever workaround lets iPhone 18 Pro Max skirt battery shipping max power limits
content:
The iPhone 18 Pro Max has a battery with more capacity than permitted to ship. To get around that, Apple is using a combination of hardware, software, and user authentication to slip under the regulatory wire.

iPhone 18 Pro Max
Customers began receiving devices on September 18. An Apple support document published the same day explains why the iPhone 18 Pro Max arrives with a battery capacity restriction in place.
At full capacity, the iPhone 18 Pro Max battery exceeds 20 watt-hours, putting it above a threshold that brings extra shipping requirements in most countries and regions. Apple uses firmware to keep the battery below 20 Wh while the phone moves through its factory and shipping network.
The restriction disappears automatically once the owner activates the iPhone, restoring access to the battery's full rated capacity, reports The Verge on Monday.
